desc: AARO is the Department of Defense's authoritative office for UAP, established by memorandum of Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks on 15 July 2022 and announced 20 July 2022. The memorandum disestablished the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group, directed the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAP Task Force and transfer its data and materials to AARO, and placed AARO under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. Congress then codified it in the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for FY2023, signed 23 December 2022, with statutory authority and reporting obligations now at 50 U.S.C. 3373 and 3373a. In summer 2023, weeks after David Grusch testified, Hicks pulled the office out of the USD(I&S) chain and made its director report directly to her. Read as containment, AARO's design is the point: a single office with department-wide UAP cognizance, staffed at 'several dozen' personnel, without subpoena authority, without an independent press function, reporting to the deputy head of the department whose special access programmes it would have to penetrate to answer the question it exists to answer. Its outputs are consistent across three directors: annual reports whose resolved cases are always prosaic, whose unresolved cases are always attributed to insufficient sensor data, and whose central sentence never varies - no verifiable evidence of extraterrestrial beings, activity, or technology. Its holdings reached 1,870 total UAP reports as of 30 May 2025. Its one genuine investigative product on the historical question, the Historical Record Report, stopped after Volume I; Volume II - the volume the Department told the Wall Street Journal would contain the Yankee Blue findings - remains unpublished as of August 2026. By 2026 the office had been overtaken by its own department: the PURSUE releases at war.gov/UFO put more primary UAP material into the public record in three months than AARO had in four years.

dossier.narrative:
AARO exists because Congress forced it into existence. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA required the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to stand up an office with a scope broader than the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group that the Deputy Secretary had created in November 2021. On 15 July 2022 Deputy Secretary Kathleen Hicks signed the memorandum that renamed and expanded AOIMSG into AARO. That memorandum is the founding document and it is worth reading for what it actually does. It makes AARO the authoritative office for UAP and UAP-related activities for the whole Department. It orders the Secretary of the Navy to disestablish the UAP Task Force and transfer its data, analysis and other relevant material. And it contains the sentence that matters most for this board: any DoD Component acting on behalf of the UAPTF, or who has data, analysis, contracts, or other material related to UAP, will immediately synchronize their efforts with the AARO.

That is a consolidation order. In a Department where the argument is that recovered material and its associated paperwork have been dispersed across contractors and unacknowledged compartments, an instruction that all UAP data, analysis and contracts route to a single office under USD(I&S) is the sort of instruction that can be read two ways. It is the necessary precondition for an honest accounting. It is also the necessary precondition for a controlled one.

AARO's first director was Sean Kirkpatrick, previously chief scientist at the Defense Intelligence Agency's Missile and Space Intelligence Center. He retired on 1 December 2023 having largely completed the Historical Record Report that his office published the following March. He publicly characterised David Grusch's allegations while, by his own later account, never having interviewed him. Grusch's position is that AARO never contacted him. Whichever account is correct, the resulting document is an investigation of a whistleblower's claims conducted without the whistleblower. Jon Kosloski, from the National Security Agency, took over in late 2024.

The office's own annual reporting is the best evidence about how the reporting channel functions. Under section 3373b of title 50, AARO hosts a secure mechanism for people claiming first-hand knowledge of a US Government UAP-related programme dating back to 1945. In the FY2025 report AARO discloses that between 2 June 2024 and 30 May 2025, 262 individuals used it. AARO determined 255 were out of scope. Seven warranted a request for a follow-on interview. That is a 97 percent rejection rate applied by the office whose own conduct is the subject of many of the allegations. The same report states, in language AARO chose, that the office is authorised by law to receive all UAP-related information at any level of classification regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented access programs, and that generally no restrictions, including non-disclosure agreements, prevent AARO from receiving it. AARO therefore claims the access and simultaneously reports that almost nobody who comes to it has anything worth hearing.

The FY2025 report contains a second internal tension that a hostile reader should sit with. It states flatly that to date no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials. Two sentences later it states that AARO is currently developing a formalized process for handling UAP-derived materials by an appropriate line organization, should such materials ever come into the possession of the USG, drawing on established procedures governing the recovery of foreign materiel. An office that has found nothing is building a custody chain for the nothing it has found.

The performance record is poor by the Department's own inspector general's measure. DODIG-2023-109, whose unclassified summary was released on 24 January 2024, found the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP, had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan, and had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands. The Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report.

The delivery record is worse. Volume II of the Historical Record Report, covering interviews and research from 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024, was promised in Volume I under a deadline set in section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA. By late February 2026 it had not appeared, the FY2025 annual report had not appeared, the deputy director post was vacant, and Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough, asked why AARO had not published or briefed in over a year, told DefenseScoop the office had nothing to announce at this time. Gough did confirm that AARO had been examining over 2,000 UAP cases, roughly 1,000 of which lacked sufficient data and sat in an active archive. When the FY2025 report finally issued, it carried document number 26-P-0880 and a Department of War letterhead, with an information cut-off of 30 May 2025.

The strongest single item against AARO is in its own Volume I. The report concedes that in 2021, without sufficient justification, the scope of an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and that the programme was later disestablished for lack of merit. AARO's framing is that the compartment was unwarranted and empty. The fact remains that a compartment was stood up to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and the office that told us so is the office that closed it.
openQuestions: Volume II of the Historical Record Report, statutorily promised under section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA and covering 1 November 2023 to 15 April 2024, had not been published as of the last confirmed reporting in February 2026. Its current status is unresolved on this board.

The identity of the IC Controlled Access Program whose scope AARO says was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering is not disclosed in Volume I, nor is the authority that expanded it or the authority that disestablished it.
AARO reports 255 of 262 secure-mechanism contacts as out of scope but publishes no breakdown of the scope test applied, no appeal route, and no record of which claims were referred elsewhere.

Whether AARO's claimed unrestricted access extended to unacknowledged SAPs and to contractor-held Independent Research and Development compartments, or only to programmes DoD and IC security officials volunteered, is not established by any released document.
dossier.whatItIs: The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office is the Pentagon body designated in July 2022 as the Department's authoritative office for unidentified anomalous phenomena. It was created under section 1683 of the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act, sits under the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, and absorbed the Navy's Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force. It publishes the statutory annual UAP report, runs a secure reporting mechanism for current and former government personnel, and produced the Historical Record Report.
dossier.whyImplicated: AARO is the single point through which every UAP record, contract and data holding in the Department of Defense was ordered to flow, which makes it either the instrument of disclosure or the instrument of consolidation, and the record supports the second reading. The office was given, by its own account, unrestricted statutory access to compartmented and special access material, then used that access to produce a report clearing the Department of every allegation made against it. Its own numbers show what the reporting channel actually does: of 262 people who came forward in a single year, 255 were declared out of scope and 7 were judged worth interviewing. Witnesses under oath before the House Oversight Committee have described being targeted after providing classified testimony, and one described a session he understood to be with AARO leadership as an effort to attack the credibility of UAP witnesses. AARO is on this map not as an arbiter but as a party: it holds the custody, it wrote the exoneration, and it decides who counts as a witness.

entityInfo.desc: AARO's structural problem, stated plainly: it is the only body with department-wide UAP cognizance, it has no subpoena power, no authority to compel contractor records, no independent counsel, no dedicated press function for most of its existence, and it reports to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. The DoD Inspector General found in DODIG-2023-109 that DoD components are not even required to report UAP incidents to it. Every negative finding AARO has published is therefore bounded twice over - by what a voluntary feed delivered, and by what an office inside OSD was willing to conclude about OSD. This is why the denial formula never varies and never widens: 'AARO has discovered no verifiable evidence' is literally true and answers nothing. The office's three directors have differed in tone, not in that sentence. What changed in 2026 was not AARO but the Department around it: a presidential direction, a cabinet-level declassification programme, an external science council, an abolition bill, and a subcommittee chair with a records demand.

timeline.label: FY2022 NDAA enacted
timeline.text: P.L. 117-81 creates the statutory requirement for a permanent UAP office and the reporting regime that becomes 50 U.S.C. 3373.

timeline.label: AARO established as the UAPTF's successor entity, per the ODNI 2022 Annual Report
AARO codified in statute
timeline.text: The FY2023 NDAA (P.L. 117-263) codifies AARO and its public reporting mandate at 50 U.S.C. 3373, including the annual report deadline AARO later misses.

timeline.label: aaro.mil launched
timeline.text: AARO launches its public website, initially without the mandated reporting mechanism; the secure reporting portal for USG employees and contractors follows in October 2023.

timeline.label: AARO Historical Record Report Volume I is silent on money
timeline.text: The Pentagon's report on the historical record addresses retrieval and reverse-engineering claims at length and contains no discussion of misappropriated funds, illegal contracting, independent research and development, or contractor financial arrangements. The official rebuttal does not engage the financial allegation at all.

timeline.label: AARO briefs Congress on the New Jersey drone incursions
timeline.text: A classified briefing to lawmakers on the drone incursions spreading across New Jersey and neighbouring areas; content not disclosed publicly.

timeline.label: Mellon says DoD improperly withholds unclassified UAP imagery
timeline.text: Christopher Mellon argues publicly that the Department is improperly withholding unclassified UAP imagery; AARO under Kosloski agrees to locate a specific F-18 video for declassification review.

timeline.label: AARO data standardization workshop
timeline.text: AARO holds a private workshop hosted by Associated Universities, Inc. in the Washington area on UAP data standardisation; the white paper is published in February 2026.

timeline.label: House Oversight UAP transparency hearing
timeline.text: The House Oversight Committee holds 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection', with military witnesses and new whistleblower-protection legislation under discussion.

timeline.label: 2,000 cases, half unanalysed
timeline.text: Hegseth commits to full compliance while declining a schedule. Spokesperson Sue Gough discloses AARO is examining over 2,000 cases, roughly 1,000 of which lack sufficient data and sit in an Active Archive.

timeline.label: UAP Science Advisory Council formed
timeline.text: ODNI, AARO and the White House ask Avi Loeb to assemble a 14-member scientific council to advise on resolving the nature of UAP and support a new interagency UAP Governance Board. Tim Gallaudet, who testified alongside Elizondo in 2024, is a member.
